scenario: Month-end. Four sealed findings are buried in the June data — a windfall, a lease, an overrun, and a slide. Use Copilot — Chat, Excel, or the Analyst agent — to dig each one out of the numbers and unlock the vault before the close call in 40 minutes.

rooms.title: The Windfall
rooms.narrative: Something big landed in March and nobody flagged it. One profit center's contingent commissions came in at several times budget — a carrier profit-share windfall buried in 500 rows of P&L. Find the number and the first lock opens.
labSteps: Open 'profit-center-pnl.csv' from your OneDrive lab-data copy — Excel with Copilot works; the Analyst agent is faster for a sweep across every profit center.

Build a four-element prompt: Goal (find the March contingent-commission outlier), Context (budget vs actual by profit center, insurance brokerage P&L), Expectations (a table of profit center, March contingent budget, actual, and variance, sorted by variance), Source (this file).
Filter to account = 'Contingent commissions' and month = 2026-03, then compare actual_usd to budget_usd for each profit center.
One profit center's actual is more than triple its budget. Verify before you trust it: open the underlying row and read the raw actual_usd value yourself.
The unlock code is that profit center's March contingent-commission ACTUAL in $ thousands — digits only, no commas, no dollar sign. Example format: 425
hints: Don't scan row by row — ask for variance (actual minus budget) on the contingent-commissions line only, March only, ranked. The windfall is not subtle; it dwarfs every other contingent variance that month.

It's a Florida retail profit center on the Gulf side of the state. Its March contingent budget was $94,500 and the actual came in at a bit more than three and a half times that. Enter the actual, converted to thousands.
skillsTaught: Filtering and ranking a P&L with Copilot instead of scanning it
The four-element prompt: Goal, Context, Expectations, Source
Verifying a Copilot answer against the underlying rows

rooms.title: The Lease
rooms.narrative: May's occupancy line hides a one-time hit: a lease buyout that landed in a single profit center and blew straight past budget. The controller wants the overage — not the total, the overage. Compute it and the second lock opens.
labSteps: Stay in 'profit-center-pnl.csv'. This time the account is 'Occupancy' and the month is 2026-05.
Prompt with the same four elements — but change the Expectations: you want actual minus budget per profit center, not the actual itself. Copilot answers the question you ask, so ask for the variance.
In Excel, a pivot of May occupancy with a variance column works too — ask Copilot to add the calculated column for you.
One profit center's May occupancy overage is a suspiciously round number — the signature of a one-time contractual payment, not rent drift.
The unlock code is that overage (actual minus budget) in $ thousands — digits only. Example format: 95
hints: If your candidate overage isn't a clean round number, you've computed the actual, not the variance. Subtract the budget. Every other profit center's occupancy variance that month is small and messy; the hit stands alone.
It's the Denver retail office. May occupancy actual was $234,000 against a $54,000 budget — enter the difference, in thousands.
skillsTaught: Asking for the derived number (variance), not the raw one
Adding calculated columns with Excel Copilot
Recognizing one-time items by their shape

rooms.title: The Overrun
rooms.narrative: Most variances are noise. This one is a pattern: a single profit center whose compensation line runs hot against budget every single month, January through June — roughly nine percent over, every time. Patterns need an id, not an anecdote. Name it and the third lock opens.
labSteps: Still 'profit-center-pnl.csv' — account = 'Compensation', all six months this time.

This is a consistency question, not an outlier question, so tell Copilot that in the Goal: find the profit center over budget on compensation in EVERY month Jan–Jun 2026, not the one with the biggest single miss.
Set Expectations to a month-by-month grid: profit centers as rows, months as columns, percent over/under budget in the cells. The Analyst agent handles this pivot well.
Verify like a reviewer: for your candidate, check all six months individually — one month under budget disqualifies it.
The unlock code is that profit center's id, exactly as it appears in the file, hyphen included. Example format: PC-999
hints: Ask for the count of over-budget months per profit center on the compensation line — only one scores six out of six. Big single-month misses elsewhere are decoys; consistency is the tell.
It's the Manhattan retail office — compensation runs about nine percent over budget every month, roughly $650k over for the half. Enter its profit-center id with the hyphen.
skillsTaught: Framing consistency questions vs outlier questions
Month-by-month pivots with the Analyst agent
Disqualifying candidates with a verification pass

rooms.title: The Slide
rooms.narrative: The last finding isn't one number — it's a headcount. June core commissions are softening across the book, and the CFO wants to know exactly how many profit centers finished the month below budget. Count carefully: the vault rejects sloppy denominators.
labSteps: Last pass at 'profit-center-pnl.csv' — account = 'Core commissions', month = 2026-06 only.

Count the profit centers whose June ACTUAL core commissions are below their June BUDGET. Only count rows where a June budget exists — the agency acquired mid-period has actuals but no budget, and it must not be in your count.
Spell that exclusion out in the prompt's Context; Copilot won't guess your denominator rules. Blank is not zero.
Verify: ask for the list of qualifying profit centers by name, not just the count, and spot-check two of them against the raw rows.

Corroborate with 'flash-comments.csv' — the June revenue_comments for each profit center on your list should read as under budget. A row on your list whose commentary reads over budget means you miscounted.
The unlock code is the count immediately followed by the word UNDER, no space. Example format: 7UNDER
hints: If your count is one too high, you counted a profit center with an empty June budget cell — the mid-period acquisition. A missing budget means the row is excluded, not that it's a zero budget beaten by any actual.
With the acquisition excluded, the count is an odd number between ten and twelve. Append the word from the code format, all caps, no space.
skillsTaught: Making denominator rules explicit in the prompt
Handling missing data — blank is not zero
Asking for the list behind a count before trusting it
